claims.claim: At 20 days after tamoxifen administration, EYFP-positive clones with cells reaching the outer layers of the epithelium were visible at the limbus cornea border.
claims.source: At this latter stage, EYFP-positive clones with cells reaching the outer layers of the epithelium were visible at the limbus cornea border (Figure 4E, arrowhead).
claims.evidence: Observation from lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: At 20 days after tamoxifen administration, groups of cells spanning the entire apical-basal axis of the central corneal epithelium were observed.
claims.source: At 20 DATX, we also observed groups of cells spanning the entire apical-basal axis of the central corneal epithelium (Figure 4F, arrowhead).
claims.evidence: Observation from lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: SOX9+ cells residing in the basal layer of the limbal and corneal epithelium are progenitors of the terminally differentiated cells of the corneal epithelium.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that SOX9+ cells residing in the basal layer of the limbal and corneal epithelium are progenitors of the terminally differentiated cells of the corneal epithelium.
claims.evidence: Inference from lineage tracing data showing EYFP-positive cells throughout the epithelium.

claims.claim: The first LacZ-positive cells scattered across the limbal and corneal surface appeared at 3 days after tamoxifen administration.
claims.source: We observed the first X-gal-positive cells at 3 DATX, and they were scattered throughout the entire limbal and corneal surface (Figure 4G, arrows).
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: At 5 days after tamoxifen administration, most X-gal+ cells were located in the limbal area.
claims.source: At 5 DATX, most X-gal+ cells were located in the limbal area, and by 10 DATX, the number of stained cells increased notably in this area.
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining.

claims.claim: Sox9-expressing descendant cells experience a process of proliferation in the limbus, illustrating their transient cell amplification behavior.
claims.source: These observations suggest that Sox9-expressing descendant cells experience a process of proliferation in the limbus, illustrating their transient cell amplification behavior.
claims.evidence: Inference from the increase in X-gal+ cells in the limbus over time.

claims.claim: At 45 days after tamoxifen administration, LacZ+ stripes emerging from the limbus and extending into the peripheral cornea became apparent.
claims.source: Fifteen days later (45 DATX), the limbal staining began to disperse, allowing the observation of discrete clones. Simultaneously, LacZ+ stripes emerging from the limbus and extending into the peripheral cornea became apparent (Figure 4H, 45 DATX, arrow, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: At 60 days after tamoxifen administration, circumferential clones that remained in the limbus could be appreciated.
claims.source: This situation was evident at 60 DATX, when the thickness and number of the stripes had increased. Additionally, starting at this stage, circumferential clones that remained in the limbus could also be appreciated (Figure 4H, 60 DATX, arrowheads, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: At 90 days after tamoxifen administration, three types of clones were observed: circumferential ones in the limbus, stripes originating from the limbus reaching the central cornea, and stripes without a base in the limbus.
claims.source: At 90 DATX, three types of clones were observed: circumferential ones in the limbus (Figure 4H, 90 DATX, arrowheads, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), stripes originating from the limbus, which often reached the central cornea (Figure 4H, 90 DATX, arrow, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and stripes without a base in the limbus (Figure 4H, 90 DATX, asterisk, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: At 365 days after tamoxifen administration, circumferential clones in the limbus and stripes originating from the limbus were mainly observed, albeit in reduced numbers and larger sizes.
claims.source: At 365 DATX, the first two types of clones were mainly observed, albeit in reduced numbers and larger sizes. We also observed some stripes without a base in the limbus (Figure 4H, 365 DATX, asterisk, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Altshuler et al., 2021 describe the co-existence of two separated stem populations in the limbus: the quiescent 'outer' limbus (OLB) one, adjacent to the conjunctiva, and the active 'inner' limbus (ILB) one, adjacent to the peripheral cornea.
claims.source: In this study, the authors describe the co-existence of two separated stem populations in the limbus, the quiescent 'outer' limbus (OLB) one, adjacent to the conjunctiva, and the active 'inner' limbus (ILB) one, adjacent to the peripheral cornea.
claims.evidence: Cited from Altshuler et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Sox9 shows high expression levels in outer limbus cells, and progressively weaker expression in the inner limbus, corneal basal, and corneal suprabasal clusters.
claims.source: Density plots based on gene-weighted kernel density estimation and violin plots of expression levels revealed high expression levels of Sox9 in OLB cells, and progressively weaker expression in the ILB, corneal basal, and corneal suprabasal clusters (Figure 5B, C).
claims.evidence: Analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: Strong Sox9 expression was detected in a mitotic cluster.
claims.source: We also detected strong expression for Sox9 in a mitotic cluster (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The PAGA graph revealed a strong connection between the outer limbus node and a mitotic cell population with high expression of outer limbus and stem cell markers.
claims.source: The PAGA graph revealed a strong connection between the OLB node and a mitotic cell population with high expression of OLB and stem cell markers (Gpha2, Ifitm3, Cd63, and Krt15), which, in turn, was strongly linked to a second mitotic cell cluster, in which the expression of these markers diminished while the expression of corneal markers (Krt12, Ppp1r3c, and Slurp) increased (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The expression levels of Sox9 correlated with the pseudotime graph, indicating that Sox9 expression decreases as transiently amplifying progenitors undergo progressive differentiation from limbal to peripheral corneal cells.
claims.source: Through the PAGA graph, we also observed that the expression levels of Sox9 correlated with the pseudotime graph (Figure 5E), indicating that Sox9 expression decreases as transiently amplifying progenitors undergo progressive differentiation from limbal to peripheral corneal cells.
claims.evidence: Analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: In the region corresponding to the outer limbus, most cells showed strong Sox9 expression.
claims.source: We observed that in the region corresponding to the OLB, most cells showed strong Sox9 expression.
claims.evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence analysis.

claims.claim: In the area corresponding to the inner limbus, Sox9 immunoreactivity appeared weaker in the basal layer, and no expression was detected in the suprabasal layers.
claims.source: In the area corresponding to the ILB, this immunoreactivity appeared weaker in the basal layer (corresponding to the ILB proper), and no expression was detected in the suprabasal layers (flattened cells; Figure 5F, left).
claims.evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Sox9 expression was restricted to P63-positive cells.
claims.source: Double immunofluorescence for SOX9 and P63, which is expressed in basal cells of the limbal epithelium, but not by transient amplifying cells covering the corneal surface (Pellegrini et al., 2001) revealed that Sox9 expression was restricted to P63-positive cells (Figure 5F, right).
claims.evidence: Observation from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5F, with citation to Pellegrini et al., 2001.

claims.claim: Sox9 is expressed in a basal cell population within both the outer limbus and inner limbus and its expression decreases in differentiated transient amplifying cells.
claims.source: These observations confirm that Sox9 is expressed in a basal cell population within both the OLB and ILB and that its expression decreases in differentiated transient amplifying cells.
claims.evidence: Inference from immunofluorescence observations.

claims.claim: 2816 genes were deregulated between cells exhibiting high and low expression levels of Sox9, with 137 upregulated and 2679 downregulated.
claims.source: We identified 2816 deregulated genes, 137 upregulated, and 2679 downregulated (adjusted p-value <0.05; |avg_log2FC| > 0.1; Figure 5G; Supplementary file 1I).
claims.evidence: Differential expression analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Among the upregulated genes in high Sox9-expressing cells were outer limbus markers including Gpha2, Ifitm3, and Cd63, in addition to stem cell markers such as Krt14.
claims.source: Among the upregulated genes, we found OLB markers including Gpha2, Ifitm3, and Cd63, in addition to stem cell markers such as Krt14 (Figure 5G; Supplementary file 1I).
claims.evidence: Differential expression analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Gene ontology analysis using the downregulated genes found terms related to stem cell differentiation, such as 'mitotic cell phase transition', 'autophagy', 'cell–cell junction', 'regulation of epithelial cell migration', 'regulation of cell morphogenesis' and 'stem cell differentiation'.
claims.source: Finally, we performed gene ontology analysis using the downregulated genes, and we found terms related to stem cell differentiation, such as 'mitotic cell phase transition' (Knoblich, 2008), 'autophagy' (Chang, 2020), 'cell–cell junction' (Ning et al., 2021), 'regulation of epithelial cell migration' (Puri et al., 2020), 'regulation of cell morphogenesis' and 'stem cell differentiation', as well as gene pathways involved in these processes including 'Wnt-signaling pathway', 'ERBB signaling' (Hassan and Seno, 2022), 'cytokine-mediated signaling pathway' (Korkaya et al., 2011), and 'regulation of ERK1 and ERK2 cascade' (Lavoie et al., 2020; Figure 5H; Supplementary file 1J).
claims.evidence: Gene ontology analysis of scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5H, with multiple citations.

claims.claim: The population of SOX9-negative cells is more differentiated than that of SOX9-positive cells.
claims.source: Altogether, these results suggest that the population of SOX9-negative cells is more differentiated than that of SOX9-positive cells.
claims.evidence: Inference from gene ontology analysis showing differentiation-related terms in downregulated genes.

claims.claim: Histological examination of the limbus and cornea from Sox9Δ/Δ mice at any time up to and including 100 days after tamoxifen administration did not reveal any discernible phenotypic effects.
claims.source: However, histological examination of the limbus and cornea from Sox9Δ/Δ mice at any time up to and including 100 DATX did not reveal any discernible phenotypic effects (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Observation from histological examination shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Immunofluorescence staining for SOX9 failed to reveal any differences in the number of SOX9-expressing cells between Sox9Δ/Δ mutants and controls.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence staining for SOX9 (Figure 6B) failed to reveal any differences in the number of SOX9-expressing cells between mutants and controls (Figure 6C; Supplementary file 1K; control, 5.4 ± 0.4 cells/100 µm, n = 7; mutant, 5.9 ± 0.7 cells/100 µm, n = 6; p = 0.147, Welch t test).
claims.evidence: Quantification from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claims.claim: Similar observations were made for corneal and limbal marker genes such as P63 and Pax6 in Sox9Δ/Δ mutants compared to controls.
claims.source: Similar observations were made for corneal and limbal marker genes such as P63 (Figure 6B, C; Supplementary file 1K; control, 6.1 ± 0.7 cells/100 µm, n = 6; mutant, 6.1 ± 0.7 cells/100 µm, n = 5; p = 0.147, Welch t test) and Pax6 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Quantification from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figures 6B, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Tamoxifen induces mosaic patterns of Sox9 deletion in the ocular surface, but Sox9-null cells cannot survive or proliferate as well as their wild-type neighbors and are hence outcompeted over time, leading to an essentially wild-type cornea.
claims.source: These observations are consistent with a model whereby tamoxifen induces mosaic patterns of cell Sox9-deleting in the ocular surface, but that the Sox9-null cells cannot survive or proliferate as well as their wild-type neighbors and are hence outcompeted over time, leading to an essentially wild-type cornea.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of the lack of phenotype in Sox9Δ/Δ corneas.

claims.claim: In control Sox9Δ/+-LacZ corneas, numerous discrete X-gal+ patches of different sizes spanning over the entire corneal surface were observed.
claims.source: In control Sox9Δ/+-LacZ corneas, derived from four mice we could observe numerous discrete X-gal+ patches of different sizes spanning over the entire corneal surface.
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining of control corneas.

claims.claim: In control Sox9Δ/+-LacZ corneas, a variable number of elongated stripes originating from the limbus were observed.
claims.source: In all cases, we observed a variable number of elongated stripes originating from the limbus, suggesting that they come from limbal stem cells (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: The majority of Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ corneas exhibited minimal blue staining, with only occasional, small X-gal+ spots observed.
claims.source: In contrast, the majority of Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ corneas, derived from five mice exhibited minimal blue staining, with only occasional, small X-gal+ spots observed.
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining of mutant corneas.

claims.claim: Only one Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ mutant cornea revealed the presence of an elongated stripe originating from the limbus.
claims.source: Notably, only one mutant cornea revealed the presence of an elongated stripe originating from the limbus (Figure 6E, right panels; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Observation from X-gal staining shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: A possible explanation for the clone in one Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ mutant cornea may be that spontaneous ligand-independent activity of Cre-ER fusion may have occurred in a bona fide limbal stem cell.
claims.source: A possible explanation for this clone may be that spontaneous ligand-independent activity of Cre-ER fusion may have occurred in a bona fide limbal stem cell, as previously reported (Vooijs et al., 2001; Kemp et al., 1994; Haldar et al., 2008; Dorà et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Speculation based on cited literature (Vooijs et al., 2001; Kemp et al., 1994; Haldar et al., 2008; Dorà et al., 2015).

claims.claim: There was a significant decrease in the percentage of blue-stained surface area in Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ mutant corneas compared to controls.
claims.source: This analysis confirmed a significant decrease in the mutant corneas compared to the controls (controls: n = 4 mice Sox9Δ/+-LacZ, 6.74 ± 2.33; mutants: n = 5 mice Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ, 0.85 ± 0.86; Mann–Whitney U-test, p = 0.0159; Figure 6F; Supplementary file 1L).
claims.evidence: Quantification from X-gal staining shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: During normal in vivo homeostasis, epithelial limbal and corneal stem/progenitor cells require Sox9 to maintain their clonogenic capacity.
claims.source: These results reveal that during normal in vivo homeostasis, epithelial limbal and corneal stem/progenitor cells require Sox9 to maintain their clonogenic capacity, indicating a key role for this gene in the process.
claims.evidence: Inference from mosaic analysis showing reduced clonogenic capacity in Sox9-null cells.

claims.claim: It is challenging to determine the contribution of Müller glial cells and RPE cells to the final Sox9 mutant retinal phenotype.
claims.source: Since Sox9 is expressed in MG and RPE cells (Poché et al., 2008), it is challenging to determine the contribution of each cell type to the final mutant phenotype.
claims.evidence: Acknowledgment of experimental limitation, with citation to Poché et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Previous studies on Sox9-mutant mice focused on the developing retina and are not useful for understanding how the absence of Sox9 in Müller glial and RPE cells in the adult eye leads to retinal degeneration.
claims.source: Previous studies on Sox9-mutant mice have not described any eye phenotype similar to the one we report here. The main reason is probably that these studies focused on the developing retina and are therefore not useful for understanding how the absence of Sox9 in MG and RPE cells in the adult eye leads to the retinal degeneration observed in our Sox9-deficient adult mutants.
claims.evidence: Comparison with previous literature and explanation of novelty.

claims.claim: In mice with DTA-induced ablation of Müller glial cells, a wave of cell apoptosis was observed in the outer nuclear layer but not in the other retinal layers.
claims.source: In mice with a DTA-induced ablation of MG cells, a wave of cell apoptosis was observed in the ONL but not in the other retinal layers (Shen et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from Shen et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In mice with DTA-induced ablation of RPE cells, the major retinal abnormality was the formation of regions of photoreceptor rosetting with very mild degeneration of the photoreceptors.
claims.source: In the first case, the major retinal abnormality was the formation of regions of photoreceptor rosetting with very mild degeneration of the photoreceptors (Longbottom et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Cited from Longbottom et al., 2009.

claims.claim: In Sox9 mutant mice, photoreceptor rosetting was not observed in the outer nuclear layer, but massive apoptosis in this retinal layer was observed.
claims.source: In our mutant mice, we did not observe photoreceptor rosetting in the ONL, but a massive apoptosis in this retinal layer.
claims.evidence: Observation from the study, contrasting with cited literature.

claims.claim: Continuous expression of Sox9 in Müller glial cells is necessary for normal function and/or survival of this cell type.
claims.source: Thus, we favor the hypothesis that continuous expression of Sox9 in MG cells is necessary for normal function and/or survival of this cell type.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of data favoring a specific hypothesis.

claims.claim: In the absence of Sox9, Müller glial cells undergo massive retinal gliosis, and they cannot provide structural, metabolic, and functional support to the other retinal cells, leading to a massive loss of photoreceptors followed by the depletion of other retinal cell types.
claims.source: In the absence of Sox9, MG cells undergo massive retinal gliosis, and they cannot provide structural, metabolic, and functional support to the other retinal cells, leading to a massive loss of photoreceptors followed by the depletion of other retinal cell types.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of data proposing a mechanistic model.

claims.claim: Sox9 expression is upregulated in Müller glial cells after retinal light damage in rats.
claims.source: In agreement with this, Sox9 expression is upregulated in MG cells after retinal light damage in rats (Wang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from Wang et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The retinal phenotype in Sox9 mutant mice is much more severe than the one observed in both DTA-induced transgenic lines.
claims.source: However, the retinal phenotype we report here is much more severe than the one observed in both DTA-induced transgenic lines.
claims.evidence: Comparison of phenotypes between the current study and cited literature.

claims.claim: The combined deletion of Sox9 in both Müller glial and RPE cells may cause a more severe phenotype than the individual cell type-specific mutants.
claims.source: This could be due to the different efficiency of Cre-induced recombination, but also to the fact that the combined deletion of Sox9 in both MG and RPE may cause a more severe phenotype than the individual cell type-specific mutants.
claims.evidence: Speculation about the cause of phenotype severity.

claims.claim: Sox9 and Otx2 cooperate to regulate visual cycle gene expression in the RPE.
claims.source: Notably, Sox9 and Otx2 cooperate to regulate visual cycle gene expression in the RPE (Masuda et al., 2014), and loss of Otx2 specifically in the adult RPE leads to secondary photoreceptor degeneration through non-cell autonomous mechanisms (Housset et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from Masuda et al., 2014 and Housset et al., 2013.

claims.claim: RPE-specific deletion of Sox9 does not induce retinal degeneration and in fact results in Otx2 upregulation.
claims.source: However, RPE-specific deletion of Sox9 does not induce retinal degeneration and in fact results in Otx2 upregulation (Masuda et al., 2014; Goto et al., 2018; Cohen-Tayar et al., 2018), suggesting that Sox9 is not an upstream regulator of Otx2 in this context.
claims.evidence: Cited from Masuda et al., 2014; Goto et al., 2018; Cohen-Tayar et al., 2018.

claims.claim: No retinal abnormality has been described in patients with a mutation in SOX9.
claims.source: To our knowledge, no retinal abnormality has been described in patients with a mutation in SOX9 (see Hejtmancik and Daiger, 2020).
claims.evidence: Statement based on review of literature, with citation to Hejtmancik and Daiger, 2020.

claims.claim: Campomelic dysplasia patients are mostly heterozygous for SOX9 and show early postnatal lethality, so a retinal degeneration phenotype in adulthood was either overlooked or not addressed.
claims.source: This is probably because CD patients are mostly heterozygous for SOX9 and show early postnatal lethality, so a retinal degeneration phenotype in adulthood was either overlooked or not addressed.
claims.evidence: Speculation about why retinal phenotypes have not been reported in CD patients.

claims.claim: SOX9/Sox9 has a complex regulatory landscape.
claims.source: However, SOX9/Sox9 has a complex regulatory landscape (Bagheri-Fam et al., 2006; Despang et al., 2019), and mutations in its regulatory region have been associated with tissue-specific human phenotypes (Wunderle et al., 1998; Benko et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2015; Kurth et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Cited from Bagheri-Fam et al., 2006; Despang et al., 2019; Wunderle et al., 1998; Benko et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2015; Kurth et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Transgenic mice carrying a human enhancer located around 500 kb upstream of SOX9 revealed enhancer activity in the eye.
claims.source: In this context, transgenic mice carrying a human enhancer located around 500 kb upstream of SOX9 revealed enhancer activity in the eye (Sreenivasan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from Sreenivasan et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Screening of the SOX9 regulatory region may provide new molecular mechanisms underlying idiopathic cases of retinal degeneration.
claims.source: Thus, screening of the SOX9 regulatory region may provide new molecular mechanisms underlying idiopathic cases of retinal degeneration.
claims.evidence: Speculation about potential clinical implications.

claims.claim: Trajectory analysis of limbal and corneal scRNA-seq data revealed that Sox9 is highly expressed in a cell population characterized by the expression of stem cell markers (Gpha2, Ifitm3, Cd63, and Krt14).
claims.source: Trajectory analysis of limbal and corneal scRNA-seq data revealed that Sox9 is highly expressed in a cell population characterized by the expression of stem cell markers (Gpha2, Ifitm3, Cd63, and Krt14), and that its expression gradually decreases as these cells enter mitosis and differentiate into suprabasal corneal cells.
claims.evidence: Analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Sox9 expression gradually decreases as limbal stem cells enter mitosis and differentiate into suprabasal corneal cells.
claims.source: Trajectory analysis of limbal and corneal scRNA-seq data revealed that Sox9 is highly expressed in a cell population characterized by the expression of stem cell markers (Gpha2, Ifitm3, Cd63, and Krt14), and that its expression gradually decreases as these cells enter mitosis and differentiate into suprabasal corneal cells.
claims.evidence: Analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: There was a substantial proliferation of Sox9-expressing descendant cells, leading to a significant increase in their numbers within the first 10 days after the initiation of tamoxifen treatment.
claims.source: Consistent with this, we observed a substantial proliferation of Sox9-expressing descendant cells, leading to a significant increase in their numbers within the first 10 days after the initiation of the TX treatment.
claims.evidence: Observation from lineage tracing experiments.

claims.claim: Sox9 was expressed exclusively in epithelial basal cells, while Sox9-expressing descendant cells were observed throughout the entire corneal epithelium.
claims.source: The fact that Sox9 was expressed exclusively in epithelial basal cells, while Sox9-expressing descendant cells were observed throughout the entire corneal epithelium, indicates that many Sox9-expressing descendant cells experience a decline in Sox9 expression, initiating their differentiation into cells that proliferate, migrate, and differentiate into suprabasal corneal cells, thus contributing to the maintenance of corneal homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Observation from lineage tracing experiments.

claims.claim: Many Sox9-expressing descendant cells experience a decline in Sox9 expression, initiating their differentiation into cells that proliferate, migrate, and differentiate into suprabasal corneal cells, thus contributing to the maintenance of corneal homeostasis.
claims.source: The fact that Sox9 was expressed exclusively in epithelial basal cells, while Sox9-expressing descendant cells were observed throughout the entire corneal epithelium, indicates that many Sox9-expressing descendant cells experience a decline in Sox9 expression, initiating their differentiation into cells that proliferate, migrate, and differentiate into suprabasal corneal cells, thus contributing to the maintenance of corneal homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Inference from lineage tracing observations.

claims.claim: The persistence of some small clones of LacZ+ Sox9Δ/Δ cells in the limbal and corneal epithelia shows that Sox9 is not absolutely required for the contribution of cells to the limbal and ocular epithelium.
claims.source: The persistence of some small clones (including a radial stripe) of LacZ + Sox9△/△ cells in the limbal and corneal epithelia of CAGG-CreERTM;Sox9flox/flox; Rosa26-LacZ mice nevertheless shows that Sox9 is not absolutely required for the contribution of cells to the limbal and ocular epithelium, but that the lack of Sox9 significantly impairs the ability of mutant cells to compete with wild-type cells.
claims.evidence: Observation from mosaic analysis.

claims.claim: The lack of Sox9 significantly impairs the ability of mutant cells to compete with wild-type cells in the limbal and corneal epithelia.
claims.source: The persistence of some small clones (including a radial stripe) of LacZ + Sox9△/△ cells in the limbal and corneal epithelia of CAGG-CreERTM;Sox9flox/flox; Rosa26-LacZ mice nevertheless shows that Sox9 is not absolutely required for the contribution of cells to the limbal and ocular epithelium, but that the lack of Sox9 significantly impairs the ability of mutant cells to compete with wild-type cells.
claims.evidence: Observation from mosaic analysis.

claims.claim: Cell competition would explain why, in contrast to the whole-mount LacZ analysis, Sox9-null cells were not detected in tissue sections of Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ eyes.
claims.source: This competition would explain why, in contrast to the whole-mount LacZ analysis, Sox9-null cells were not detected in tissue sections of these eyes.
claims.evidence: Inference from mosaic analysis observations.

claims.claim: A recent preprint describes a study that confirms the stem-clonogenic potential of Sox9-positive limbal epithelial cells.
claims.source: A recent preprint (Rice et al., 2024) describes a study that confirms the stem-clonogenic potential of Sox9-positive limbal epithelial cells.
claims.evidence: Cited from Rice et al., 2024.

claims.claim: A recent preprint reports that conditional deletion of Sox9 leads to abnormal corneal epithelial differentiation and squamous metaplasia in the central cornea.
claims.source: That study also reports that conditional deletion of Sox9 leads to abnormal corneal epithelial differentiation and squamous metaplasia in the central cornea.
claims.evidence: Cited from Rice et al., 2024 (implied from context).

claims.claim: The squamous metaplasia phenotype reported in a recent preprint was not observed in the current study, possibly because the mosaic nature of the model may allow for rescue of normal Wnt and Notch signaling by wild-type cells, preventing transdifferentiation.
claims.source: This phenotype was not observed in our study but is explicable because of the mosaic nature of our model, which may allow for rescue of the normal Wnt and Notch signaling by wild-type cells, preventing transdifferentiation (Menzel-Severing et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Explanation for discrepancy with cited literature, with citation to Menzel-Severing et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Long-lived circumferential clones that never exited the limbus are similar to those produced by outer limbus cells.
claims.source: We also observed long-lived circumferential clones that never exited the limbus. These latter clones are similar to those produced by OLB cells, as recently shown in lineage-tracing experiments, which predominantly self-renew and minimally contribute, if at all, to the formation of lineages maintaining the corneal epithelium during homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Observation from lineage tracing, with comparison to cited literature.

claims.claim: Outer limbus cells predominantly self-renew and minimally contribute to the formation of lineages maintaining the corneal epithelium during homeostasis.
claims.source: These latter clones are similar to those produced by OLB cells, as recently shown in lineage-tracing experiments, which predominantly self-renew and minimally contribute, if at all, to the formation of lineages maintaining the corneal epithelium during homeostasis.
claims.evidence: Cited from recent lineage-tracing experiments (implied from context, likely Altshuler et al., 2021 or Farrelly et al., 2021).

claims.claim: In response to corneal injury, outer limbus cells proliferate and play an essential role in wound healing.
claims.source: However, in response to corneal injury, OLBs proliferate and play an essential role in wound healing (Altshuler et al., 2021; Farrelly et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Cited from Altshuler et al., 2021 and Farrelly et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Sox9 is highly expressed in the outer limbus cluster.
claims.source: Consistent with this, we saw that Sox9 is highly expressed in the OLB cluster.
claims.evidence: Analysis of scRNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Previous studies utilizing an H2B-GFP/K5tTA mouse model have shown that Sox9 is expressed in a corneal quiescent/slow-cycling cell population.
claims.source: Furthermore, previous studies utilizing an H2B-GFP/K5tTA mouse model have shown that Sox9 is expressed in a corneal quiescent/slow-cycling cell population (Parfitt et al., 2015), and wound healing assay using a human corneal organ culture revealed an increase in the number of SOX9+ cells in both activated limbal and re-grown corneal epithelial cells (Menzel-Severing et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Cited from Parfitt et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Wound healing assay using a human corneal organ culture revealed an increase in the number of SOX9+ cells in both activated limbal and re-grown corneal epithelial cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, previous studies utilizing an H2B-GFP/K5tTA mouse model have shown that Sox9 is expressed in a corneal quiescent/slow-cycling cell population (Parfitt et al., 2015), and wound healing assay using a human corneal organ culture revealed an increase in the number of SOX9+ cells in both activated limbal and re-grown corneal epithelial cells (Menzel-Severing et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Cited from Menzel-Severing et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The number and extension of the limbal circumferential clones diminished in Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ corneas, indicating that Sox9 may also control the proliferation of outer limbus stem cells.
claims.source: We also observed that the number and extension of the limbal circumferential clones diminished in Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ corneas, indicating that Sox9 may also control the proliferation of OLB stem cells.
claims.evidence: Observation from mosaic analysis.

claims.claim: In the retina, Müller glial cells play a vital role in providing structural and metabolic support.
claims.source: In the retina, MG cells play a vital role in providing structural and metabolic support.
claims.evidence: Established knowledge about Müller glial cell function.

claims.claim: Sox9 is essential for the maintenance and survival of Müller glial cells.
claims.source: Here, we demonstrate that Sox9 is essential for the maintenance and survival of MG cells.
claims.evidence: Conclusion from experimental data in the study.

claims.claim: Notch signaling, which is critical for the maintenance of retinal progenitor cells and the specification of Müller glial cells, regulates Sox9 expression.
claims.source: In this context, previous studies have shown that Notch signaling, which is critical for the maintenance of retinal progenitor cells and the specification of MG cells (Mills and Goldman, 2017), regulates Sox9 expression.

results.result: Sox9 deletion in adult mice leads to severe retinal degeneration characterized by loss of Müller glial cells and complete depletion of the photoreceptor layer. The severity of the phenotype correlates with the efficiency of Sox9 inactivation, with extreme phenotypes observed only when Sox9 is inactivated in at least 80% of expressing cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C41-C43, C50-C55 collectively demonstrate retinal degeneration upon Sox9 deletion with histological, immunofluorescence, and quantitative evidence. The correlation between recombination efficiency and phenotype severity (C50-C51) is supported by SOX8/SOX9 co-staining data (C48-C49) and statistical analysis (C52). The mosaic nature of tamoxifen-induced recombination explains phenotypic variability.

results.result: Sox9 deletion results in loss of multiple retinal cell types including both cone and rod photoreceptors, ganglion cells, amacrine cells, and horizontal cells, indicating that Sox9 is required for maintenance of diverse retinal neuronal populations in the adult eye.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 are supported by immunofluorescence data for multiple cell-type-specific markers (opsins, RHO, BRN3A, PAX6, AP2α) with statistical significance (p<0.05 for all comparisons). The data demonstrate widespread retinal degeneration beyond the initially described photoreceptor and Müller glial loss.

results.result: Photoreceptor cells undergo apoptosis following Sox9 deletion, as evidenced by TUNEL staining predominantly in the outer nuclear layer. The apoptotic process may occur acutely within a narrow temporal window.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by TUNEL assay data showing statistically significant increase in apoptotic cells (p=0.028, zero-inflated Poisson model). However, C64 is speculative regarding the temporal dynamics. The variability in TUNEL+ cell counts across samples suggests either acute apoptosis or sampling limitations, but the overall conclusion of photoreceptor apoptosis is well-supported.

results.result: Müller glial cells undergo progressive reactive gliosis in Sox9-deficient retinas, as demonstrated by increased GFAP expression that extends from the ganglion cell layer through the entire retinal thickness in severe phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 are supported by GFAP immunofluorescence showing progressive extension of GFAP+ processes correlated with phenotype severity, with statistically significant quantification (p=0.024, Mann-Whitney U-test, n=4 controls, 10 mutants). The interpretation of reactive gliosis is consistent with established markers and cited literature (C65).

results.result: Sox9 is expressed in basal limbal and corneal epithelial cells that function as progenitors for terminally differentiated corneal epithelial cells. Lineage tracing reveals that Sox9+ cells undergo transient amplification in the limbus and give rise to two types of long-lived clones: circumferential clones in the limbus and radial stripes extending into the cornea.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C84 are supported by comprehensive lineage tracing experiments using Sox9-EYFP and Sox9-LacZ reporter mice with temporal analysis from 3 to 365 days after tamoxifen. The data demonstrate Sox9+ cell proliferation, migration patterns, and long-term clonal dynamics. The interpretation that Sox9+ cells are progenitors (C77) is well-supported by the observation of labeled cells throughout the epithelial layers.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq analysis reveals that Sox9 is highly expressed in outer limbus basal cells and progressively decreases during differentiation toward corneal epithelial cells. High Sox9 expression correlates with stem cell markers (Gpha2, Ifitm3, Cd63, Krt14), while low Sox9 expression is associated with differentiation-related gene ontology terms.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C97 are supported by comprehensive scRNA-seq analysis including UMAP clustering, pseudotime trajectory analysis (PAGA), differential gene expression (2816 genes, adjusted p<0.05), and gene ontology enrichment. The analysis is validated by immunofluorescence (C90-C92) showing Sox9 expression patterns consistent with the scRNA-seq data. The interpretation that Sox9-negative cells are more differentiated (C97) is well-supported by GO terms.

results.result: Mosaic analysis reveals that Sox9 is essential for limbal stem cell clonogenic capacity. Sox9-null cells are outcompeted by wild-type cells during normal homeostasis, resulting in significantly reduced clonal contribution to the corneal epithelium (p=0.0159).
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C108 are supported by mosaic analysis using Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ mice showing dramatic reduction in X-gal+ clones compared to controls (6.74±2.33% vs 0.85±0.86%, p=0.0159, Mann-Whitney U-test). The lack of histological phenotype (C98-C100) combined with reduced clonal contribution (C107) supports the cell competition model (C101). The interpretation that Sox9 is required for clonogenic capacity (C108) is well-supported, though C106 is speculative.

results.result: The authors propose that Sox9 is necessary for Müller glial cell function and survival, and that loss of Sox9 leads to Müller glial dysfunction, reactive gliosis, and secondary degeneration of photoreceptors and other retinal neurons. This phenotype is more severe than DTA-induced ablation of either Müller glia or RPE alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C118 represent mechanistic interpretation and comparison with prior work. While the phenotypic observations are well-supported (C113, C117), the mechanistic model (C114-C115) is inferential. The authors acknowledge the challenge of distinguishing Müller glial vs RPE contributions (C109) and note that combined deletion may cause more severe phenotypes (C118), but this remains speculative. The comparison with DTA models (C111-C112, C117) is valid but the underlying mechanism is not definitively established.

results.result: The authors discuss potential clinical relevance, noting that retinal abnormalities have not been reported in SOX9 mutation patients (campomelic dysplasia), possibly due to early lethality. They speculate that mutations in SOX9 regulatory regions might underlie idiopathic retinal degeneration cases.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C125 are primarily speculative regarding clinical implications. C121 correctly states that retinal abnormalities have not been reported in CD patients, and C122 provides a reasonable explanation (early lethality). However, C125 is purely speculative without supporting data. The discussion of SOX9 regulatory complexity (C123-C124) is supported by citations but the clinical relevance remains hypothetical.

results.result: Trajectory analysis and lineage tracing demonstrate that Sox9 expression decreases as limbal stem cells enter mitosis and differentiate into suprabasal corneal cells, with Sox9+ descendant cells contributing to corneal homeostasis through proliferation, migration, and differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C130 integrate scRNA-seq trajectory analysis (C126-C127) with lineage tracing observations (C128-C129) to support the conclusion that Sox9 expression declines during differentiation (C130). The data are consistent and mutually reinforcing, though C130 involves some inference about the mechanism of homeostasis maintenance.

results.result: The persistence of small Sox9Δ/Δ clones indicates that Sox9 is not absolutely required for limbal/corneal epithelial contribution, but significantly impairs competitive fitness of mutant cells relative to wild-type cells, explaining the lack of Sox9-null cells in tissue sections.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C133 are supported by the mosaic analysis data showing rare small clones in Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ mice (C104-C105) versus abundant clones in controls (C102-C103). The cell competition model (C132-C133) provides a coherent explanation for the discrepancy between whole-mount and section analysis, though the mechanism of competition is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: The authors compare their findings to a recent preprint (Rice et al., 2024) that reports squamous metaplasia upon Sox9 deletion, which was not observed in the current study. They attribute this discrepancy to the mosaic nature of their model allowing rescue by wild-type cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C136 discuss concordance and discordance with concurrent work. C134 is a straightforward citation, C135 reports a finding from the preprint, and C136 provides a speculative explanation for the discrepancy. The explanation is plausible but not directly tested, making this evaluation uncertain.

results.result: Sox9 is highly expressed in outer limbus cells, which predominantly self-renew during homeostasis but proliferate in response to injury. Sox9 may control outer limbus stem cell proliferation, as evidenced by reduced circumferential clones in Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ corneas.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C143 integrate the current study's findings (C137, C140, C143) with prior literature on outer limbus cell behavior (C138-C139, C141-C142). The observation of reduced circumferential clones in Sox9Δ/Δ-LacZ mice (C143) supports a role for Sox9 in outer limbus cell proliferation, though the mechanism is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: The authors propose that Sox9 fulfills multiple roles in the retina including regulation of structural protein expression (COL1, GFAP) and promotion of cell survival through anti-apoptotic activity, similar to its role in Sertoli cells. This suggests a general role for Sox9 in adult tissue maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C151 represent mechanistic interpretation integrating current findings with prior literature. While C145 is supported by the data, the specific molecular mechanisms (C146-C148) are cited from other studies and not directly demonstrated here. The parallel with Sertoli cells (C150) is cited, and the generalization to multiple tissues (C151) is inferential. The model is plausible but not definitively proven.

results.result: In the cornea, Sox9 appears to regulate proliferation and differentiation of limbal stem/progenitor cells through engagement with BMP, Notch, Shh, and Wnt signaling pathways, with high Sox9 expression associated with stem cell markers and declining expression during differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C155 integrate the current study's scRNA-seq and lineage tracing data (C153) with prior in vitro studies on signaling pathways (C154). The association between Sox9 expression and stem cell markers is well-supported by the scRNA-seq data (C153), though the signaling pathway interactions (C154) are cited from prior work rather than directly demonstrated here.

results.result: Through functional analyses in mice, the authors demonstrate that Sox9 acts as an essential maintenance factor preventing retinal degeneration and promotes differentiation of limbal cells in the cornea.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C157 represent the main conclusions of the study, summarizing the retinal and corneal findings. Both are well-supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including conditional deletion, lineage tracing, scRNA-seq analysis, and mosaic analysis.

results.result: Sox9 expression in the adult eye is restricted to retinal pigmented epithelium cells, Müller glial cells, and limbal/corneal basal epithelia, following downregulation during neuronal differentiation from an earlier expression in retinal progenitor cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C24-C26, C45 describe Sox9 expression patterns based on established literature (Poché et al., 2008; Muto et al., 2009; Masuda et al., 2014) and confirmed by the current study's immunofluorescence data. The expression pattern is well-documented and serves as the foundation for the functional studies.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on retinal and corneal anatomy, including the structure and function of photoreceptors, Müller glial cells, and limbal epithelial stem cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C19 represent established anatomical and physiological knowledge about the eye, appropriately cited from the literature. These claims provide necessary context for the experimental work but do not constitute novel findings.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior literature on SOX9 function in development and adult tissue homeostasis, including its role in campomelic dysplasia, stem cell maintenance in various tissues, and previous studies on Sox9 in retinal and corneal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C40 represent a comprehensive literature review establishing the knowledge gap that motivates the current study. All claims are appropriately cited and accurately represent prior work. C40 correctly identifies that the in vivo role of Sox9 in adult retinal and corneal maintenance was unknown prior to this study.

results.result: Retinal degeneration was never observed in control mice, making the presence of the Pde6brd1 allele unlikely, though the authors acknowledge that definitive exclusion would require PCR genotyping.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 addresses an important control regarding the Pde6brd1 retinal degeneration allele. While the absence of degeneration in controls is reassuring, the authors acknowledge in the manuscript that definitive exclusion requires PCR genotyping, which was not performed. This represents a minor limitation in experimental rigor.

results.result: Sox9 deletion in adult mice causes severe retinal degeneration characterized by loss of Müller glial cells and complete depletion of the photoreceptor layer. The severity of the phenotype correlates with the efficiency of Sox9 inactivation, with extreme phenotypes observed only when Sox9 is inactivated in at least 80% of expressing cells. Müller glial cell numbers are significantly reduced in mutant retinas, with some regions completely devoid of these cells.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. The editor states 'the data at hand convincingly support the main conclusions,' Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors show that Sox9 is essential for retinal integrity, and its null mutation causes the loss of the outer nuclear layer,' and Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'molecular marker analysis provides strong evidence of Mueller cell loss and photoreceptor degeneration' and 'phenotype severity nicely correlates with the efficiency of Cre-mediated Sox9 depletion.'

results.result: Sox9 deletion leads to loss of both rod and cone photoreceptors, as well as reduction in ganglion cells, amacrine cells, and horizontal cells, indicating that Sox9 loss causes degeneration of multiple retinal neuronal populations beyond photoreceptors and Müller glia.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'the authors then show that this absence of the ONL is due to apoptosis of photoreceptors and a reduction in the numbers of other retinal cell types such as ganglion cells, amacrine cells and horizontal cells.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'molecular marker analysis provides strong evidence of Mueller cell loss and photoreceptor degeneration.' No reviewer challenges these findings.

results.result: Sox9Δ/Δ mice show numerous TUNEL+ cells mainly in the outer nuclear layer, indicating photoreceptor apoptosis. The difference in apoptotic cells between control and mutant retinas is statistically significant, though photoreceptor apoptosis may occur acutely within a narrow temporal window.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly confirms 'the authors then show that this absence of the ONL is due to apoptosis of photoreceptors.' The statistical significance and temporal dynamics are part of the careful analysis that Reviewer 2 praises, noting 'careful analysis suggests that two degeneration phenotypes (mild and severe) are detected.' No concerns are raised about the apoptosis data.

results.result: In the absence of Sox9, Müller glial cells undergo progressive gliosis, as evidenced by increased GFAP expression that extends from the ganglion cell layer through the entire retina in mutants with extreme phenotypes. GFAP signal is statistically significantly increased in mutant retinas, indicating that Müller glial cells become reactive upon Sox9 deletion.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'they also describe that Müller Glia undergoes reactive gliosis by upregulating the Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'molecular marker analysis provides strong evidence of Mueller cell loss and photoreceptor degeneration.' The gliosis findings are part of the convincing evidence that all reviewers accept.

results.result: Sox9 lineage tracing experiments demonstrate that Sox9 is expressed in a basal limbal stem cell population that forms two types of long-lived clones: circumferential clones in the limbus and radial stripes extending from the limbus to the cornea. SOX9+ cells in the basal layer of limbal and corneal epithelium are progenitors of terminally differentiated corneal epithelial cells, with Sox9-expressing descendant cells undergoing proliferation in the limbus.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 confirms 'the authors then show that Sox9+ progenitors proliferate and differentiate to generate the corneal cells through Sox9 lineage-tracing experiments.' Reviewer 2 states 'lineage tracing revealed that Sox9 is expressed in a basal limbal stem cell population that supports stem cell maintenance and homeostasis' and praises 'a clever genetic tracing strategy uncovers a critical role for Sox9 in limbal stem cell differentiation.' The editor affirms the study 'uncover[s] a dual role for a transcription factor (Sox9) in stem cell differentiation.'

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis reveals that Sox9 shows high expression in outer limbus cells with progressively weaker expression in inner limbus, corneal basal, and suprabasal clusters. Sox9 expression correlates with pseudotime, decreasing as cells differentiate from limbal to corneal cells. Sox9 is expressed in basal cells positive for stem cell markers (Gpha2, Ifitm3, Cd63, Krt14) and is restricted to P63-positive cells. Differential expression analysis shows upregulation of stem cell markers and downregulation of differentiation-related genes in high Sox9-expressing cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'they validate Sox9 expression and characterize its dynamics in limbal stem cells using an existing single-cell RNA sequencing dataset.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'lineage tracing revealed that Sox9 is expressed in a basal limbal stem cell population.' The scRNA-seq analysis is part of the comprehensive characterization that reviewers find convincing, with no concerns raised about these molecular findings.

results.result: Mosaic analysis comparing Sox9Δ/Δ and control corneas shows that Sox9 deletion causes limbal stem/progenitor cells to lose their clonogenic capacity. While histological examination of Sox9Δ/Δ corneas shows no discernible phenotype and no difference in SOX9+ or P63+ cell numbers, mosaic LacZ analysis reveals significantly reduced blue-stained surface area in mutants. Sox9-null cells persist in small clones but are outcompeted by wild-type cells over time, indicating Sox9 is essential for competitive fitness though not absolutely required for cell contribution.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly confirms 'the authors show that Sox9 deletion causes progenitor cells to lose their clonogenic capacity by comparing the sizes of control and Sox9-null clones.' Reviewer 2 states 'mosaic analysis confirmed that Sox9 is essential for the differentiation of limbal stem cells.' The editor affirms the study demonstrates Sox9's role 'in stem cell differentiation.' The mosaic analysis is praised as 'clever' by Reviewer 2.

results.result: The study demonstrates that Sox9 is required for maintenance of retinal integrity and limbal stem cell differentiation in the adult mouse eye. Continuous Sox9 expression in Müller glial cells is necessary for their normal function and survival. In its absence, Müller glial cells undergo gliosis and cannot provide structural, metabolic, and functional support to other retinal cells, leading to massive photoreceptor loss followed by depletion of other retinal cell types. In the cornea, Sox9 promotes differentiation of limbal cells.
results.evaluation: The editor states 'the authors uncover a dual role for a transcription factor (Sox9) in stem cell differentiation and prevention of retinal degeneration' and 'the data at hand convincingly support the main conclusions.' Reviewer 1 confirms 'Hurtado et al. underline the importance of Sox9 function in retinal cells.' Reviewer 2 states 'the study highlights that Sox9 is critical for both retinal integrity and the differentiation of limbal stem cells in the adult mouse eye.' All reviewers accept these main conclusions.

results.result: The study addresses a knowledge gap: while previous studies examined Sox9 in retinal and corneal development, its specific in vivo contributions to maintenance and regeneration of these tissues in adult mammals remained unknown. Previous Sox9-mutant studies focused on the developing retina and are not useful for understanding how Sox9 absence in adult Müller glial and RPE cells leads to retinal degeneration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly praises the novelty, stating 'inducible genetic approaches in the adult mouse nervous system are rare and difficult to carry out. Here, the authors employ tamoxifen-inducible mouse mutagenesis to uncover the functional roles of Sox9 in the adult mouse eye.' The editor confirms the study 'informs the transcriptional mechanisms that promote stem cell differentiation and prevent degeneration in the adult eye.' The adult-specific approach is a key strength acknowledged by reviewers.

Peer reviewers explicitly affirm these findings, with Reviewer 2 noting 'phenotype severity nicely correlates with the efficiency of Cre-mediated Sox9 depletion.'
